clue.text: 'Old-fashioned', old university with 'tense' old fellow? 'Tense? That hurts!'

parts.note: O is a standard abbreviation for old
U is the abbreviation for university
T is the grammar abbreviation for tense
O again for old
F is the abbreviation for fellow
T again, the grammatical abbreviation for tense
the cry someone gives when something hurts

explanation.surface: A fusty old don, stiff with tension, winces when anyone touches his sore spot.
explanation.walkthrough: The quotation marks chop the clue into a run of tiny abbreviations followed by an exclamation; each piece is a short standard abbreviation, and the cry of pain finishes the answer OUT OF TOUCH.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone behind the times has lost contact with current trends, an idiomatic way of calling them dated.

clue.text: It provides beer and some toasties

definitions.note: loose: an oast dries the hops that go into beer

indicators.note: only some of the following word is used, so a run of letters sits inside it

parts.note: the second to fifth letters of the word

explanation.surface: A pub that serves both beer and grilled cheese sandwiches.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is generous: an OAST is the kiln, often in a Kent oast house, where hops are dried before brewing. Toasties are toasted sandwiches.
explanation.definitionFit: Hop kilns dry the crop that flavours bitter, so the building is a step in brewing.

clue.text: Rubber cushion for bore that's outspoken

indicators.note: something outspoken is spoken out, so we go by the sound of the word

parts.note: to bore someone is to tire them

explanation.surface: A rubber pad bought for a tactless, tiresome person.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bore' looks like a noun for a tedious person, but it is the verb meaning to weary. The British spelling TYRE matches the sound of tire.
explanation.definitionFit: A pneumatic wheel covering is an air-filled rubber ring that softens the ride, a playful description.

clue.text: Penalise a vacuously natured fop? OK

parts.note: to penalise is to impose a monetary charge
taken as written

indicators.note: emptied out, the word keeps only its shell with nothing inside

parts.note: first and last letters only
a fop is a vain, showy man

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether to punish an empty-headed, good-humoured fop, and gets an approving 'OK'.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Vacuously natured' reads like a description of the fop's character, but it tells you to hollow the word out. The question mark separates the wordplay from the one-word definition.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is a cheerful idiom meaning everything is all right, a jaunty equivalent of okay.

clue.text: Where nurses go in direction of front

definitions.note: read as ON WARDS, a place phrase rather than an adverb
definitions.meaning: first reading: hospital staff work on the wards

explanation.surface: Directions for nurses heading towards the front of a building.
explanation.walkthrough: Split the answer as ON WARDS and it says where nurses work; read whole, it is an adverb of forward movement.
explanation.definitionFit: Going forward means advancing towards what lies ahead, the ordinary adverb sense of the word.

clue.text: Painter's title describing witch

indicators.note: to describe a shape is to draw round it, so one word goes around another

parts.note: a title or name is what you call something
a hag is an ugly old witch

explanation.surface: An artist names a painting after the witch it shows.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Describing' suggests a picture's caption, but in geometry to describe a circle is to draw round it. Call as a noun means a name or title only loosely.
explanation.definitionFit: Marc Chagall was a Russian-French modernist artist famous for dreamlike floating figures.

clue.text: Part of hospitality industry: foolish people in retirement

indicators.note: retiring means withdrawing or going back, so the word is turned round

parts.note: saps are gullible fools

explanation.surface: Hotels and resorts are run by daft folk who have retired.
explanation.walkthrough: The colon makes the second half look like a description of hospitality workers; it is wordplay instead.
explanation.definitionFit: Health resorts with pools and treatments are businesses within the leisure and hotel trade.

clue.text: House plant's site? In a pot, strangely!

indicators.note: something done strangely is done oddly, so the letters come out in an unexpected order

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Where does a houseplant live? Oddly enough, in a pot.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface pretends to be a mock-surprised answer to a riddle, but the plant's home is the fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: The red-bracted Christmas favourite is a common indoor potted plant in winter.

clue.text: Serve salad, tossed: it contains capers and anchovies

indicators.note: tossing mixes things up thoroughly, so the letters get jumbled

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Instructions for serving a mixed salad that includes capers and anchovies.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is descriptive rather than a synonym: it lists two typical ingredients of the sauce.
explanation.definitionFit: Italian green sauce is made from parsley, olive oil, capers and salted fish, so the recipe fits.

clue.text: Therapist with discussion that offers protection

definitions.note: describes the wrapping, which is a noun

parts.note: slang for a psychiatrist
W is short for with
a rap is an informal talk, as in a rap session

explanation.surface: Talking therapy as a safeguard for mental health.
explanation.walkthrough: 'With' looks like a joining word but supplies a single letter. A rap as a frank chat is chiefly American slang.
explanation.definitionFit: Tight plastic film sealed round goods keeps them clean and undamaged, so it guards them.

clue.text: Saudi money? Retreat, retreat!

indicators.note: an order to go back, so the word goes backwards

parts.note: a lair is a den or hideaway

explanation.surface: A panicked cry to fall back when Saudi cash is at stake.
explanation.walkthrough: The same word does two jobs: first as a noun meaning hideaway, then as the command telling you to turn it around.
explanation.definitionFit: The riyal, also spelt this way, is the national currency unit of Saudi Arabia.

clue.text: Resentful, quiet, Warhol's concocted thing involving pop?

parts.note: bitter means resentful
the call for silence
Andy Warhol, the pop artist

explanation.surface: A sulky, silent account of something Andy Warhol cooked up in the Pop Art movement.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pop' points to Warhol's Pop Art but means fizzy lemonade. Bitter is a British draught beer, and a shandy mixes beer with lemonade.
explanation.definitionFit: The drink is a mixed concoction of ale topped up with lemonade, which Britons call pop.

clue.text: Resort site: Arcadia (it's part of the Med)

indicators.note: read as re-sort: sort again into a different order

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A holiday resort called Arcadia on the Mediterranean coast.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Resort' looks like a holiday destination, matching the Mediterranean setting, but split as re-sort it is the instruction to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: The arm of water between Italy and the Balkans is an inlet of the Mediterranean.

clue.text: Characteristic of a hive of activity?

definitions.text: Characteristic of a hive of activity?

parts.note: surface reading: a bustling place full of work
setter's reading: the trait of an insect living in a literal hive

explanation.walkthrough: A 'hive of activity' is an idiom for a bustling place; the question mark invites taking the hive literally and thinking of its industrious inhabitant.
explanation.definitionFit: The simile describes someone hardworking and occupied, the trait for which honey-making insects are proverbial.

clue.text: Promises Caesar: 'Sun's to rise'

indicators.note: to rise up is to revolt, and rebellious letters break out of order

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written, dropping the apostrophe

explanation.surface: Caesar pledges, like an emperor-god, that the sun will come up.
explanation.walkthrough: The colon makes the words after it look like Caesar's quoted promise, but they and his name are the fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: Pledges and guarantees given to reassure someone are both nouns meaning firm undertakings.

clue.text: They'll deliver packages 'on 15th March, perhaps' — plus points!?

parts.note: UPS, the parcel delivery company
the Ides of March fell on the 15th in the Roman calendar

explanation.surface: Couriers delivering on the Ides of March, with the bonus of a good outcome.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Perhaps' warns that 15 March is just one example of the Ides, which fell on the 13th in some months. UPS is the United Parcel Service.
explanation.definitionFit: Advantages or favourable aspects of a situation are its good sides, an everyday plural noun.

clue.text: Beatles song, The French Bird, live

parts.note: le is French for the
a tit is a small songbird
to be is to exist or live

explanation.surface: A Beatles track title that sounds like a live recording of a French band.
explanation.walkthrough: The italics make the second half look like a band name; it breaks into three pieces. The tit is a familiar British garden bird.
explanation.definitionFit: The 1970 single by Paul McCartney's group is one of the band's best-known recordings.

clue.text: U8? That sounds like a threat

indicators.note: the clue asks us to judge by how the characters are said rather than written

parts.note: the letter and the digit read out run together

explanation.surface: A text-speak message read out and taken as menacing.
explanation.walkthrough: Say the letter and the number quickly and the second word slurs into the warning; 'That sounds like a threat' is both indicator and definition.
explanation.definitionFit: The exclamation warns of coming retribution, an idiom meaning just wait until I get you.

clue.text: Material from Falstaff et al.

indicators.note: taken from within the following words, so the letters are lifted out of them

parts.note: runs across the end of the name and the next two words

explanation.surface: Fabric sourced from Shakespeare's Falstaff and his companions.
explanation.walkthrough: Falstaff is Shakespeare's fat knight; 'et al.' means and others. The letters run from the end of his name into the abbreviation.
explanation.definitionFit: A crisp woven silk fabric used for dresses is a kind of cloth.

clue.text: Bore seeing vehicle with bumpy ride

parts.note: a car is a vehicle

indicators.note: a bumpy journey jolts things about, so the letters get thrown out of order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A dull person watching a car jolt along a rough road.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bore' looks like a noun for a tedious person; it is the past tense of the verb to bear.
explanation.definitionFit: To bear a load is to transport it, so the past tense of bear matches transported.

clue.text: Greek character (averse to wine)

parts.note: chi is a letter of the Greek alphabet
anti means opposed to

explanation.surface: A Greek person who dislikes wine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Character' suggests a person in a story, but here it is a letter. The brackets make the wine look like the character's dislike.
explanation.definitionFit: The Tuscan red from Italy is a well-known variety of alcoholic drink made from grapes.

clue.text: Cold — it's often covered in ice!

definitions.note: read as STAND OF FISH, a noun phrase
definitions.meaning: second reading: a fishmonger's display, laid out on crushed ice

explanation.surface: Something chilly that is usually coated with frost.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cold' and 'ice' both seem to be about temperature; split the answer as STAND OF FISH and the second half is a fish counter.
explanation.definitionFit: A distant, reserved manner is socially frosty, the figurative sense of unfriendly aloofness.

clue.text: Mercian king taking most of entrails

indicators.note: most but not all, so the final letter is dropped

parts.note: offal is the edible innards of an animal

explanation.surface: An Anglo-Saxon king helping himself to the bulk of the innards.
explanation.walkthrough: Offa ruled Mercia in the eighth century and is remembered for Offa's Dyke on the Welsh border; Mercia was a kingdom of the English Midlands.
explanation.definitionFit: He was the powerful eighth-century ruler of the Anglo-Saxon realm in central England.

clue.text: Britpoppers' endless promotional material

indicators.note: without an end, so the final letter is cut off

parts.note: a blurb is publicity text, as on a book jacket

explanation.surface: A Britpop band's never-ending stream of publicity.
explanation.walkthrough: Blur were a leading 1990s Britpop band, rivals of Oasis; the possessive makes the band look like a describer of the material.
explanation.definitionFit: The group fronted by Damon Albarn was one of the defining acts of nineties British guitar music.

clue.text: Rugby player's retreat

definitions.meaning: first meaning: one of the players behind the forwards

explanation.surface: A rugby player falling away from the action.
explanation.walkthrough: The possessive suggests the retreat belongs to the player; it is just joining two meanings.
explanation.definitionFit: In rugby the backs line up behind the scrum, and backing away is withdrawing.

clue.text: Telling Everyman: 'Wave Union flag, nothing to lose'

indicators.note: to wave something is to move it to and fro, so the letters are moved about
losing something means it is taken away from what remains

parts.note: the setter refers to himself
taken as written
nothing is zero, shaped like the letter

explanation.surface: The setter, waving a Union Jack, rallies the crowd that there is nothing to lose.
explanation.walkthrough: A setter's pseudonym stands for the first person. The Union flag is the British national flag; one O comes out before the remaining letters are shuffled.
explanation.definitionFit: A telling look or remark is significant and expressive, conveying a great deal.

clue.text: At heart, Balearic cassette offers calm

indicators.note: the heart is the centre, so only the middle letters count

parts.note: the two central letters of the eight
the two central letters of the eight

explanation.surface: A tape of chilled Ibiza music is soothing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'At heart' covers both words; Balearic music is the chilled dance genre associated with Ibiza.
explanation.definitionFit: Tranquillity and freedom from strain mean the same as relaxed comfort, so the nouns match.

clue.text: Victorian allusive narrative — it tickles your fancy? Accordingly, I recommend, to start with, ____!

indicators.note: the start of each word is all that is kept, so only initials count

parts.words: Victorian allusive narrative — it tickles your fancy? Accordingly, I recommend
parts.note: the initial letter of each of the ten words

explanation.surface: A recommendation of a satirical Victorian novel that might appeal, with a blank to fill in.
explanation.walkthrough: The blank invites you to supply the title; the first letters of the ten words before the indicator spell it. Thackeray's novel takes its title, an allusion, from Bunyan's Pilgrim's Progress.
explanation.definitionFit: Thackeray's 1848 novel is a famous nineteenth-century English satire whose name borrows from Bunyan.
